headline: Britain and the EU agree to cut food checks

sources.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports (BBC)
UK and EU agree deal to remove Brexit checks on food and animal products (The Guardian)
UK and EU agree draft food deal to scrap post-Brexit export checks (Business Matters)

chunks.text: After Britain left the European Union in 2020, a change known as Brexit, its fresh [[sausages]] and some [[shellfish]] were {{shut out}} of the [[EU market]]. That could change. On November 3, 2026, news outlets reported a 200-page [[draft]] deal on food between the two sides, not yet [[approved]]. It would {{do away with}} most [[food checks]]. It would also {{bring back}} passports for British pets traveling to the EU.

verbs.correct: To stop something from entering a place
verbs.wrong: To make something cheaper in stores
verbs.why: The new fence shuts out stray dogs. Strict rules shut out many foreign products. After Brexit, fresh British sausages were shut out of the EU market.

verbs.correct: To end or remove something completely
verbs.wrong: To wrap something in clean paper
verbs.why: Many schools do away with paper tests. Some airlines do away with printed tickets. The draft deal would do away with most food checks.

verbs.wrong: To make people pay a higher fee
verbs.why: Some stores bring back old products when customers ask. Many schools bring back uniforms after a few years. The deal would also bring back passports for British pets traveling to the EU.

chunks.text: Under current rules, British food companies {{fill out}} forms and pay 200 British pounds for a health certificate, an [[official paper]] saying food is safe. One small company paid a [[vet]] 140 pounds to [[inspect]] each [[shipment]], so it {{gave up}} selling yogurt to the EU. One truck was {{held up}} for 27 days at a French [[port]] without the right papers, a transportation industry leader told lawmakers. Britain's main farmers' group says food sales to the EU have fallen [[by a third]] since Brexit.

verbs.correct: To complete a form with information
verbs.wrong: To read a form very carefully
verbs.why: Patients fill out a form at the doctor's office. Students fill out an application for college. British companies fill out forms to sell food to the EU.

verbs.correct: To stop trying to do something
verbs.why: Many people give up learning an instrument after a few months. He gives up when a puzzle gets hard. One small company gave up selling yogurt to the EU because it was losing money.

verbs.correct: To make someone or something late
verbs.wrong: To weigh a load of goods
verbs.why: Heavy traffic often holds up the bus. Bad weather holds up flights in winter. One truck was held up for 27 days at a French port.

chunks.text: [[In return]] for fewer checks, Britain would follow EU rules on food, plants and animals. It would have to {{keep up with}} those rules whenever they change. The government says the deal will [[eventually]] be worth 5.1 billion pounds a year to the [[economy]]. A major business group expects it to {{pay off}} through [[lower costs]]. But some politicians who support Brexit have {{pushed back}}. The leader of the Conservative Party, which opposes the government, says following EU rules would take Britain [[backward]].

verbs.correct: To stay equal with something that changes
verbs.wrong: To write a rule for other people
verbs.why: Wages do not always keep up with prices. Small companies work hard to keep up with new technology. Britain would have to keep up with EU food rules whenever they change.

verbs.correct: To bring good results in the end
verbs.wrong: To make a new law for business
verbs.why: Hard study usually pays off at exam time. A long training plan pays off on race day. A major business group expects the deal to pay off through lower costs.

verbs.correct: To oppose a plan or decision
verbs.wrong: To read a plan before a meeting
verbs.why: Workers push back when a company changes their hours. Parents push back against new school rules. Some politicians who support Brexit have pushed back against the deal.

chunks.text: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham says most people would expect him to seek the best deal he can. Leaders are expected to {{sign off on}} the deal at a [[summit]], a formal meeting, on November 20. The Guardian newspaper reports that the changes may not {{kick in}} until early 2028. Britain must first change its food laws to match the EU's.

verbs.wrong: To print copies of a document
verbs.why: The manager signs off on every large purchase. A doctor signs off on each test report. EU and British leaders are expected to sign off on the deal on November 20.
The medicine kicks in after about 20 minutes. The heating kicks in when the room gets cold. The Guardian reports that the changes may not kick in until early 2028.

mainIdea.s: Britain and the EU have settled a draft deal to end most food checks that began after Brexit. Britain would follow EU food rules in return, and leaders are expected to approve it in November.
mainIdea.why: The deal would do away with most food checks. Britain would keep up with EU rules, and leaders are expected to sign off on it on November 20.

mainIdea.s: The EU has agreed to drop its controls on British products without asking for anything. Britain keeps its own standards, so companies can start selling sausages across the border this winter.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Britain would have to follow EU rules in return. The changes also may not kick in until early 2028.

mainIdea.s: British farmers have asked their government for new payments after a poor potato harvest. Officials in London say they will study the request and announce a decision at a meeting next spring.
mainIdea.why: This is about a draft food deal between Britain and the EU, which would do away with most food checks and bring back pet passports.

tf.s: The draft deal would do away with most checks on food.
tf.why: The deal would do away with most food checks, so fresh sausages could be sold in the EU again.

tf.why: It would bring back passports for British pets traveling to the EU.

tf.s: Under the deal, the EU would follow British food rules.
tf.why: It is the other way around. Britain would follow EU rules and keep up with them whenever they change.

tf.s: British companies now pay for a health certificate on food sent to the EU.
tf.why: Companies fill out forms and pay 200 British pounds for a health certificate, an official paper saying that food is safe.

tf.s: Some politicians who support Brexit have pushed back against the deal.
tf.why: They have pushed back. The leader of the Conservative Party says following EU rules would take Britain backward.

tf.s: The changes will kick in right after the November summit.
tf.why: Leaders are expected to sign off on the deal in November, but the changes may not kick in until early 2028.

lines.text: Did you hear about the food deal between Britain and the EU? Fresh British sausages were {{shut out}} of the EU market after Brexit. This draft deal could change that.
So the two sides want less [[red tape]]?
Right. It would {{do away with}} most food checks. Right now, companies {{fill out}} so many forms.
I've heard those companies really have to [[jump through hoops]].
They do. One small company paid a vet to inspect every shipment, so it just {{gave up}}.
That sounds like [[more trouble than it's worth]].
And one truck was {{held up}} for 27 days at a French port.
Poor driver. Does the deal help regular people too?
Yes, it would {{bring back}} passports for British pets.
Dog owners will love that. What does Britain have to do in exchange?
Follow EU food rules and {{keep up with}} any changes.
So that's [[give and take]]. Is everyone happy with it?
No. Some politicians who support Brexit have {{pushed back}}.
So when will leaders {{sign off on}} it?
They're expected to do that on November 20, but the changes may not {{kick in}} until 2028.
Britain has to change its food laws first.
Well, I guess the sausages will have to wait.
